title: Future Research Areas
summary: The final CS329A lecture recaps the quarter, then frames the self-improvement loop as bottlenecked on three fronts (reasoning-chain diversity, robust verification, human-curated task/prompt selection) and anchors each to a paper: multi-agent fine-tuning for diversity, DeepSeek-Math V2 meta-verification, and Absolute-Zero-style self-proposed tasks. The second half pivots to efficiency for intelligence: exploding cloud compute demand (~1200x, 160T to 1.3Q tokens), the charge that ~77% of queries are locally servable, the intelligence-per-watt metric (5.3x over two years), and the trend toward local/edge inference. It closes with open directions: foundational principles of test-time scaling, the synthetic-data flywheel, continual learning (weights vs memory vs infinite context), hybrid serving infra (Hydrogen, Tokamak), and energy as the primary resource.

sections.title: Course recap: from verifier loops to agents
sections.problem: The quarter spanned test-time scaling, train-time scaling, open-ended search, agentic workflows, and evaluation; without a recap the connections between the topics are lost.
sections.why: Each topic fed the same self-improvement loop -- verifiers produce feedback and rewards, and RL plus search let models hill climb -- with an exploration branch where a model may explore a definable space.
sections.how: Recap the arc in order: test-time and train-time scaling, open-ended evolution (Alpha Evolve), end-to-end tool-use workflows with retrieval and memory, next-generation evaluation, and guest lectures on post-training, multi-model agents, robotics, and reasoning.
sections.detail:
The instructor recaps the quarter. The class opened with LLMs and the past year's shift toward test-time scaling and train-time scaling via self-improvement, where the fundamental loop is driven by verifiers, feedback from running them, rewards, and reinforcement learning plus search algorithms that let models hill climb on math and coding.

  • Then evolutionary strategies and open-endedness: not only reward-driven loops but letting models explore when the exploration space can be defined -- Alpha Evolve and similar techniques.
  • Then end-to-end agent workflows with tool use: models interact with environments and tools; multi-step tasks require knowledge bases, hence retrieval and memory, better planning and multi-step reasoning.
  • Next-generation model evaluation and what capabilities drive it; guest lectures on post-training, multi-model agents, robotics, and reasoning.
  • A guest lecturer framed symbolic techniques under tool use as a way to add to synthetic data, another trend the instructors flag.

Why it matters: the field moves so fast that today's material starts becoming history by the next offering, yet the basic techniques compound because new work builds on them.

sections.title: From LLM to agent: workflow framing and lecture organization
sections.problem: LLMs by themselves are often not powerful enough to drive a full goal, so agents are still largely handwritten workflows, and it is unclear how the orchestration pieces fit together.
sections.why: An agent generalizes an LLM by having a goal, interacting with an environment, collecting feedback, and correcting its own steps -- which requires planning, multi-step reasoning, self-correction, and self-improvement.
sections.how: Describe the orchestration stack (LLMs, verifiers and LLM-judges, tool calls, parallel search) and frame the final lecture as key ideas from papers split between the self-improvement side and the efficiency-for-intelligence side.
sections.detail:
The class is titled self-improving agents, so the focus is the agent, not just the LLM. An agent is a generalization of an LLM: it has a goal, interacts with the environment, collects feedback, and uses that feedback to correct its steps -- a system that directs its own processes, uses tools, and accomplishes a goal.

  • Today's LLMs are often not powerful enough to drive a full goal alone, so workflows are still largely handwritten: you orchestrate LLMs, verifiers (needed for reward), LLM-as-judge verifiers, tool calls, and parallel search over LLM calls.
  • Coding agents are the notable case where the workflow is increasingly driven by the model itself.
  • Because the workflow chases a goal, it needs planning, multi-step reasoning, self-correction when heading the wrong way, and continued capability improvement -- the self-improvement aspect.

This final lecture covers future research areas, organized as key ideas from papers that span the self-improvement side and the efficiency-for-intelligence side, both of which the instructors consider the next important directions.

sections.title: Three bottlenecks of the self-improvement loop
sections.problem: Test-time scaling (multiple samples, majority voting) and train-time scaling still work mostly in narrow domains such as math and coding, and prompts are chosen statically by humans.
sections.why: Three root causes bound the loop: a single model produces low-diversity reasoning chains even at high temperature, verification is hard (outcome-only checking saturates benchmarks), and task/prompt curation requires scarce domain experts.
sections.how: Survey one research direction per bottleneck -- multi-agent generation for diversity, meta-verification, and self-proposed tasks at the edge of ability -- then pivot to the efficiency half and ask what 'intelligence per unit cost' means.
sections.detail:
Two lessons recap: test-time scaling (multiple samples, majority voting) and train-time scaling (feedback from the inference loop turned into rewards that drive self-improvement). The limitation is that this remains narrow -- mostly math and coding.

  • Bottleneck 1 -- diversity. How do you get generalization across domains and keep reasoning chains diverse enough to keep driving the loop? A single LLM emits near-duplicate chains even at high temperature.
  • Bottleneck 2 -- verification. Robust verification or meta-verification that checks what went into the reasoning chain is valuable; outcome reward models saturate math benchmarks while hiding invalid reasoning.
  • Bottleneck 3 -- data. Prompts entering training are selected very statically and require humans; how does the loop pick the right data to drive itself?

The second half shifts to efficiency for intelligence -- intelligence per what? -- because self-improvement means much more inference per unit of useful output. Each theme is anchored to a paper that, given how fast the field moves, might itself be taught next time.

sections.title: Multi-agent fine-tuning: debate for diverse reasoning
sections.problem: Iterative synthetic-data fine-tuning (generate, filter with rejection sampling, SFT on the good ones; STaR-style) stops improving after a few or tens of iterations.
sections.why: A single LLM generates near-duplicate solutions even at high temperature, so the training set lacks diversity and the loop hits a ceiling -- unlike internet-scale pretraining data, which was diverse because humans produced it over a long period.
sections.how: Train specialized generation and critic agents: generation agents produce diverse initial solutions, critic agents evaluate/refine across debate rounds, responses are summarized across agents, and majority-vote-matching outputs are used for SFT.
sections.detail:
First paper: multi-agent fine-tuning for self-improvement with diverse reasoning chains. Motivation: pre-training compresses internet-scale data, but instruction fine-tuning needs real human preferences for good vs bad responses. The synthetic alternative is iterative fine-tuning with rejection sampling: generate solutions, filter incorrect ones, fine-tune on the good ones (variants such as STaR, optionally adding reasoning chains).

  • Problem: a single LLM's solutions are highly similar, so gains stall after a few or tens of iterations; internet data was diverse because it accumulated from humans over time.
  • Mechanism: multiple specialized agents. Generation agents (fine-tuned from the same base model) produce diverse initial solutions; critic agents evaluate and refine over multiple debate rounds.
  • Each later step summarizes all other agents' responses (summarize with a model or concatenate) and includes that in generating the next response; the critic critiques the updated set rather than a single response.
  • Critics are fine-tuned on trajectories that start correct and are corrected through debate, learning to contrast correct vs incorrect answers. A naive version uses different models or prompts as a 'poor man's' diversity.

Caveat: because fine-tuning is involved, you are restricted to open-source base models.

sections.title: Multi-agent fine-tuning results and transfer
sections.problem: It is not obvious that multi-agent debate actually sustains hill climbing, or whether it merely produces noisier data that still saturates.
sections.why: Single-agent fine-tuning sharpens the generating distribution; spreading generation across specialized agents keeps the response distribution wide, so each round still carries new signal.
sections.how: Measure iterations vs negative log likelihood (performance proxy) and embedding dissimilarity (diversity), compare single- vs multi-agent, and test transfer to an adjacent domain (GSM8K).
sections.detail:
Results are plotted as fine-tuning iterations (x) against negative log likelihood (a performance proxy) and embedding dissimilarity (higher = more diverse).

  • For two open-source models, performance keeps climbing across iterations of multi-agent fine-tuning; Llama 3 appears more responsive to the technique.
  • The more interesting plot: response diversity stays high across iterations on a math dataset, while single-agent fine-tuning accuracy collapses or stops improving.
  • The experiment was repeated on math across three open-source models; multi-agent methods improved even over multiple fine-tuning steps, whereas single-agent fine-tuning plateaued.
  • Transfer: on an adjacent domain, GSM8K, the fine-tuned agents also scored higher (an older paper, so absolute numbers are not high).

Takeaway: self-improvement requires diverse reasoning chains; one way to generate them is multiple models or agents, and the benefit generalizes beyond the in-domain dataset. The lecture then names the open challenge: how to push the improvement frontier more reliably using only verifiable domains.

sections.title: Verification bottleneck: DeepSeek-Math V2 meta-verifiers
sections.problem: Outcome reward models only check whether the final answer matches ground truth, so math benchmarks saturate even when the reasoning is invalid -- fatal for theorem proving, which needs rigorous step-by-step derivation.
sections.why: LLMs are trained mostly on quantitative reasoning, emit mathematically invalid proofs, and when asked to verify declare those invalid proofs valid (LLM-as-judge fails). Expert humans can spot gaps, but process reward models are hard to build and human labeling does not scale.
sections.how: DeepSeek-Math V2 asks humans to identify proof flaws with no reference solution, trains LLMs to imitate that issue-spotting, and adds a meta-verifier that audits whether the verifier's flagged issues are real and whether the score follows.
sections.detail:
Second bottleneck: verification. Model outputs are hard to verify; typically you look only at the outcome -- an outcome reward model checks whether the final answer matches ground truth. This saturates math benchmarks even when the reasoning is wrong; a correct answer can hide an invalid derivation.

  • Current RL assumes the final answer matches ground truth, but LLMs trained mostly on quantitative reasoning emit proofs that can be mathematically invalid.
  • LLM-as-judge fails here: asked to verify, the model claims incorrect proofs are valid. Expert humans instead spot gaps -- a step that does not follow, or a bad reference -- but process reward models are hard to build and human labeling does not scale.
  • DeepSeek-Math V2 proposes meta-verifiers: humans identify issues in proofs with no reference solutions, LLMs learn to imitate that issue-spotting, and a meta-verifier reviews the verifier's analysis.
  • Architecture: a generator produces proofs, a verifier scores them on a 0.5-1 scale from identified issues, and the meta-verifier checks whether flagged issues are real and whether the score follows. Generator and verifier then co-improve in a loop.

sections.title: Meta-verification results and the verification recipe
sections.problem: Does adding a meta-verifier actually raise proof quality, and can the labeling loop escape dependence on human experts?
sections.why: Once seeded with human issue identification, the meta-verifier can automate labeling; generator and verifier form a co-improving loop where better proofs harden the verifier and a stronger verifier improves the generator.
sections.how: Benchmark the generator-verifier loop on IMO and CNML problems, track proof score across iterations and pass@1/best@32, then abstract the recipe: reference-free verifiers, a meta-verification block, and an incentive for deliberate reasoning.
sections.detail:
Once seeded with human-identified issues, labeling can be automated -- the meta-verifier learns the skill, so you no longer depend on experts. The loop builds on GRPO over DeepSeek V3 base models and is benchmarked on IMO and CNML problems.

  • Across 8 iterations, the proof score keeps climbing with pass@1 just from the iterative verification-generation loop.
  • With best@32 (pick the best of 32 generated proofs), the model approaches ~42% on the IMO short list 2024 -- promising as a hill-climbing technique.
  • Insight: the best proofs earn higher verification scores, the generator learns to separate high-quality from flawed proofs, and self-verification yields a better improvement loop.
  • Caveat: still limited to domains where verification is relatively easy.

The generalizable recipe: (1) LLM-based verifiers that identify issues without reference solutions; (2) a meta-verification block to reduce hallucinated issues; (3) an added incentive for the generator to maximize quality through deliberate reasoning.

sections.title: Data barrier: self-proposed tasks (Absolute Zero)
sections.problem: SFT uses human-curated reasoning traces and RLVR needs expert-curated question-answer pairs (math/IMO experts, strong coders); as models surpass humans, the supply of experts and suitably hard tasks becomes the limiting factor.
sections.why: Learning needs tasks at the edge of current ability -- neither trivial nor impossible -- and human supply of such tasks cannot keep pace with model capability.
sections.how: A single model both proposes and solves tasks in a coding abstraction with three task types (deduction, abduction, induction); the proposer is conditioned on past generated examples to promote diversity.
sections.detail:
Third bottleneck: what data or prompts should we train on? The current stack uses human-curated reasoning traces (SFT) or expert-curated question-answer pairs (RLVR), which requires domain experts -- math experts for math, IMO experts for IMO problems, strong software coders for code. As models surpass human intelligence, finding enough experts and hard tasks becomes limiting.

  • Proposal (the Absolute Zero line): a single model both proposes tasks and solves them, going to the other extreme from human curation -- essentially no external human data needed, provided some verification exists.
  • Domain: coding. Three task types: deduction (generate a program and input; the environment executes to produce the output); abduction (similar -- generate program and inputs, environment computes outputs); induction (sample an existing program, generate new inputs plus a natural-language description of the function; the environment executes and decides whether the direction is right).
  • The proposer is conditioned on past generated examples, explicitly added to the prompt, to promote diversity.

sections.title: Proposer rewards, validation, and evolving curriculum
sections.problem: A self-proposed loop can generate garbage or reward-hacked tasks, and there is no inherent signal for which generated tasks are worth training on.
sections.why: Selecting tasks the solver sometimes passes and sometimes fails maximizes learning signal, and code tasks can be validated objectively (execution, safety, determinism).
sections.how: Reward proposals by solver success (0 if never solved, else 1 minus average success rate), keep a buffer of (input, output, program) triplets with success/fail counts, and validate program integrity, safety, and determinism before training.
sections.detail:
How tasks are selected and validated:

  • The proposer gets a reward from solver success. If the solver's success rate is zero, reward is zero; otherwise it is 1 minus average success rate. This selects moderate difficulty -- tasks the solver sometimes passes and sometimes fails -- maximizing learning signal.
  • The goal is optimal task difficulty at the current model weights: as the model becomes more capable, the proposer must learn to generate harder problems.
  • A task buffer stores (input, output, program) triplets with success/fail counts; the proposer samples references from it.
  • Before entering the training pipeline, proposed tasks are validated: program integrity (execute and check for errors), safety checks, and determinism (same inputs must yield identical outputs -- possible in code). This prevents the proposer from hacking garbage tasks.

Net effect: an evolving curriculum, a play on synthetic data generated in-loop at the task level, where proposer and solver co-adapt. It clearly relies on curriculum learning and on having some form of verification available.

sections.title: Self-proposed task results and emerging behaviors
sections.problem: It is unclear whether a self-proposed curriculum can match or beat human-curated data, and whether any gains stay in-domain.
sections.why: Because proposer and solver are mildly adversarial but co-improving, validated self-generated tasks act as an on-the-fly synthetic-data source whose difficulty rises with capability.
sections.how: Compare against models trained on tens of thousands of expert examples, track complexity and diversity metrics over iterations, and evaluate on both coding and math benchmarks.
sections.detail:
Results: the loop hill climbs on coding benchmarks with no human-curated prompt data, and outperforms models trained on tens of thousands of expert examples.

  • Complexity metrics increase over time, as expected when the proposer keeps raising task difficulty.
  • Diversity of programs and answers improves when the loop is set up correctly, and the proposer generates harder tasks as training progresses.
  • Proposer and solver are slightly adversarial -- a game-theoretic flavor -- but overall help each other improve.
  • Despite hill climbing only on self-proposed code tasks, they see strong performance on both coding and math benchmarks -- surprising, but explainable from other results in the field.
  • Larger models get bigger gains relative to smaller models.

Takeaway: task selection should not bottleneck on human data, as long as some verification exists, and the technique clearly depends on curriculum learning. This is another promising lever for continuing to hill climb the self-improvement loop.

sections.title: Discussion: Swirl, transferability, and model scale
sections.problem: Is the self-improvement data flywheel a general phenomenon or specific to one task family?
sections.why: Self-generated data appears to improve the model on the generation task and to transfer to adjacent tool-use skills, and larger models absorb the flywheel better.
sections.how: Compare with Swirl (step-by-step RL with synthetic data): training on multi-hop QA with retrieval improved other tool calling (Python, math) and vice versa; note larger-model gains on the RL optimization side.
sections.detail:
A student connects this to Swirl (step-by-step RL with synthetic data) and the recurring synthetic-data flywheel pattern.

  • In Swirl, training on multi-hop question answering with retrieval made the model better at other tool calling -- e.g. calling Python to solve math problems -- and vice versa. So self-generated data improves the model on the generation task and transfers to adjacent skills.
  • Larger models seem better at absorbing this kind of data flywheel and generalizing through it, especially on the RL optimization side.
  • The instructors note the repeated trend -- model-generated training data driving generalization -- and observe that the diversity lever and the synthetic-data flywheel reinforce each other.

Implication: the open questions are how to achieve reasoning-chain diversity more reliably and how to push the improvement frontier on verifiable tasks and then transfer the gains to domains without automated verification.

sections.title: Recap of three bottlenecks and the verifiable-frontier proposal
sections.problem: Where does the self-improvement frontier go next: stay within verifiable domains, or attack the non-verifiable ones directly?
sections.why: Diversity, robust verification, and data selection are the three levers; if synthetic data on diverse verifiable tasks makes models generally smarter, that can reduce dependence on labeled data elsewhere.
sections.how: The instructors summarize the three open problems, then propose a compute-heavy experiment: push the frontier using only verifiable domains and test whether the gains generalize to domains without automated verification.
sections.detail:
Instructor summary of the three bottlenecks, then a concrete research proposal.

  • Diversity: true generalization and reasoning need diverse reasoning chains; how to achieve that remains an open problem.
  • Verification: the more the verifier loop can be broken without human bottlenecking -- building reward models is challenging -- the better; meta-verification is one route.
  • Data: only so much data can be curated by humans for which prompts go in; breaking this barrier is important for the next generation of self-improving models.

Proposal from the co-instructor: measure how far the self-improvement frontier can be pushed using only verifiable domains, where synthetic data can be generated across diverse tasks and brought back to the model. The key question is whether this makes the model generally smarter and whether it generalizes to non-verifiable domains -- potentially minimizing or removing the need for labeled data there. It is flagged as a very compute-heavy research experiment.

sections.title: Non-verifiable domains and reward hacking
sections.problem: Many valuable applications have no fast verifier: scientific discovery, chip design whose simulation takes days to yield one reward signal, chemistry requiring a wet lab, and creative work whose quality is subjective.
sections.why: RL fine-tuning and test-time scaling need rewards that arrive quickly -- ideally instant, maybe minutes to an hour -- because training takes hundreds or thousands of iterations and cannot wait days or a human in the loop; a slightly-off learned proxy invites reward hacking.
sections.how: Enumerate the non-verifiable cases and their timescales, and note that subjective rewards can be modeled, but the RL or agent will hack them if the proxy is off base.
sections.detail:
Which applications fall outside verifiable problems?

  • Scientific discovery and chip design, where a slow simulation can take days to yield a single reward signal.
  • Chemistry and bio experiments that require a wet lab: you must physically run things to see the output quality or reward.
  • Creativity and creative writing, where quality is subjective and an exact reward function is hard to design -- 'truly non-verifiable'.

The core constraint: in RL fine-tuning and test-time scaling, verifiers must be almost instant -- perhaps minutes, maybe up to an hour at the outside -- because training needs hundreds or thousands of iterations and cannot wait days or a human in the loop for each reward. These are the non-verifiable domains.

You can always model a subjective objective with a learned reward, but if the model is slightly off base the RL or agent can reward-hack it. Slow or subjective verification is therefore a structural limit on where self-improvement loops can be applied.

sections.title: Workarounds: surrogate reward models and decomposition
sections.problem: How do practitioners get a usable reward when the true verification -- simulation, wet lab, performance profiling -- is slow or unavailable?
sections.why: A learned surrogate can stand in for the expensive check inside the RL loop, but its generality is bounded by the offline data, and inaccuracy propagates into training.
sections.how: Train a separate reward model on offline data to predict simulation/experiment outcome and use it as the verification object; or decompose the problem into sub-parts with reference solutions and a knowledge base (e.g. kernel-bench performance profiling).
sections.detail:
How people attack the hard-to-verify domains:

  • Surrogate reward models. Instead of running the expensive simulation, emulation, or experiment, collect a lot of data offline and train a separate reward model that, given an input, predicts the quality of the output. Use that model as the verification object inside the RL optimization loop. Caveat: its generality is a function of how much data you have, and inaccuracy causes problems (and reward hacking).
  • Problem decomposition. Instructors cite Stanford's kernel bench-style work: compiler execution gives a pass/fail and some metrics, but reading performance profiles as complexity grows -- concatenating kernels and finding the unoptimized parts -- is a much harder problem. The common workaround is to break the problem into sub-parts, point the model at each part, and provide reference solutions in a knowledge base.

Both approaches trade verification fidelity for speed: a learned proxy is cheap but exploitable, while decomposition matches the task to current model capability instead of waiting for one model to solve the whole thing.

sections.title: Efficiency: the mainframe era and exploding compute demand
sections.problem: Self-improvement multiplies inference (sampling, debate, tool calls) just as serving demand explodes, so the cost of intelligence becomes a first-order research constraint.
sections.why: Today's largest models run on cloud because they are big, proprietary, or both, and demand is growing at rates that outrun efficiency gains.
sections.how: Frame the second half of the lecture: study model-side and hardware-accelerator-side trends to predict what inference workloads will look like, then ask whether demand can be redistributed to local devices.
sections.detail:
Azalia opens the efficiency half. Today is a mainframe era: the large models behind ChatGPT and Gemini run on cloud, not locally, because they are big, often proprietary, and even open large models are served remotely. At the same time, inference demand is exploding.

  • Google Cloud compute serving grew on the order of 1200x in roughly 12-20 months.
  • NVIDIA saw around 10x year-over-year growth.
  • Serving this demand implies data centers on the order of ~250 GW, with steadily rising energy supply needs.
  • Tokens processed on Google's side rose from 160 trillion (February last year) to 1.3 quadrillion (October this year) -- among the fastest compute growth curves in history.

Since self-improvement means far more inference per unit of output, the cost of intelligence is now a first-class constraint. The project studies both model-side and hardware-side trends to predict future workloads and asks how demand can be redistributed.

sections.title: Workload reality: most queries are simple and locally servable
sections.problem: It is assumed that all inference must go to frontier cloud accelerators, but the actual query distribution may not require them.
sections.why: From a large dataset of ChatGPT users, roughly 77% of requests are practical guidance, information, or writing -- tasks addressable by smaller/local models -- while local accelerator memory has grown ~126x since 2012 (laptops with ~100 GB, 8-bit quantized serving).
sections.how: Analyze the served workload to find what fraction is actually easy, pair it with the local-hardware trend, and define 'local' as 20B active parameters or less.
sections.detail:
The workload does not match the assumption that everything needs a frontier model.

  • From a large dataset of ChatGPT users, about 77% of requests are practical guidance, information, or writing -- tasks that smaller, local models can handle correctly.
  • Users keep asking harder questions as chatbots improve, but the vast majority of queries remain on the simpler side and are addressable by smaller models rather than large proprietary ones.
  • Meanwhile local inference accelerators improved roughly 126x in GPU memory since 2012; laptops now carry on the order of 100 GB of memory, enough to serve very large models when quantized to 8-bit (and often lower).
  • For this study, local is defined as 20B active parameters or less.

These two trends -- simpler queries and capable local hardware -- suggest a different distribution of inference, motivating the question of what role local inference can play in re-distributing demand away from H100s, TPUs, and GB200/300-class cloud accelerators.

sections.title: Intelligence per watt: metric and study design
sections.problem: Existing evaluations score capability only, so there is no systematic way to compare a local model's usefulness against its energy cost or against purpose-built enterprise accelerators.
sections.why: Local chips were designed without the assumption that LLMs would run locally, so on LLM workload efficiency they lag optimized cloud parts even as model quality and local memory improve.
sections.how: Define intelligence per watt (average task accuracy divided by average power draw), sweep 20+ models across hardware and benchmarks, and open-source the per-substrate metrics so trends can be tracked.
sections.detail:
New metric: intelligence per watt (IPW) = average task accuracy divided by the average power draw to solve the task by the model. The capability side captures the share of single-turn/reasoning queries a model can address; the efficiency side captures useful compute per watt on local hardware.

  • Study scope: 20+ local models (quantization variants, GPTQ, Llama 3, and others), across both enterprise and local accelerators.
  • Workloads: 1 million ChatGPT-sourced queries plus reasoning benchmarks -- Natural Reasoning, MMLU Pro, Super GPQA.
  • Metrics: accuracy, energy, latency, and compute, all open-sourced across model and hardware substrates.
  • Design intent: a single scalar to compare a local model's usefulness against its energy cost and against enterprise parts, since local chips were not designed assuming LLMs would run on them.

The metric makes the efficiency question concrete: not just 'how smart' but 'how much intelligence per joule'.

sections.title: Intelligence-per-watt findings and trends
sections.problem: How fast are local models and local hardware actually closing the gap, and where does the improvement come from?
sections.why: Decomposing IPW gains into model-side and hardware-side contributions shows whether the shift to edge is a model story, a chip story, or both.
sections.how: Compare the share of chat queries solved over time, benchmark Apple M4 Max against B200 on IPW, and factor the two-year gain into model and hardware components.
sections.detail:
Findings:

  • Since 2023, local models improved 3.1x on the proportion of chat queries they can solve -- a fast two-year jump -- and now address roughly 88.7% of the studied queries.
  • Local accelerators still lag on efficiency: an Apple M4 Max delivers about 1.5x lower intelligence per watt than a B200. The reason is optimization target: B200s are extremely tuned for language-model workloads, while local chips were designed for other workloads -- which is why chip-design focus has been on cloud-scale parts.
  • Overall IPW improved 5.3x over two years, decomposed into 3.1x from better models and 1.7x from more efficient hardware.

Because model capability and hardware efficiency are improving simultaneously, more traffic can plausibly move to edge devices -- laptop or phone -- over time. The trade-off is that local efficiency still trails cloud parts, so the shift is a distribution question, not a wholesale replacement.

sections.title: Future directions: test-time scaling principles, flywheel, continual learning
sections.problem: The loop works empirically, but the principles behind test-time scaling are undescribed, models cannot learn on the go, and the synthetic-data flywheel is not understood.
sections.why: Repeated sampling producing correct answers is unexplained, best practices for distilling successful trajectories are unclear, and models rely on offline data generation plus asynchronous fine-tuning unlike humans who learn continuously from successes and failures.
sections.how: Open directions: foundational principles for test-time scaling and trajectory distillation, the synthetic-data flywheel, and continual learning -- possibly via weights, memory systems, or massively longer effective context.
sections.detail:
Open directions that connect the flywheel to learning on the go.

  • Foundational principles of test-time scaling. Why does asking the same question repeatedly yield correct answers? What is the model doing, and what are the best practices to distill successful trajectories back into the model? These remain open.
  • Synthetic-data flywheel. Right now the approach is RL plus data collection plus fine-tuning; the instructors argue there is more to understand about this property and its connection to continual learning.
  • Continual learning. Humans improve continuously while solving problems; models rely on offline experience collection followed later by fine-tuning -- a mismatch. The question is what new practices let positive experiences, negative experiences, and problem-solving feed back into the model more naturally than the current asynchronous data-generation-plus-fine-tuning paradigm.

Possible mechanisms span weight updates, memory systems, and massively longer effective context -- the three are contrasted in the Q&A that follows. The course deliberately covered pre-training less than post-training and test-time scaling.

sections.title: Infrastructure, hybrid serving, and energy as the primary resource
sections.problem: The serving stack is not built for the inference pattern test-time scaling produces, and energy is becoming the binding constraint.
sections.why: Repeated sampling, generation-to-generation updates, and tool calling differ sharply from single-turn chatbot traffic, while local accelerators lag cloud parts and energy supply limits data centers.
sections.how: Build high-throughput low-latency test-time-scaling infra (e.g. Hydrogen, Tokamak), hybrid serving engines that route between local and cloud by complexity/resources, new energy-efficient architectures/kernels, and treat intelligence per watt as the target metric.
sections.detail:
The infrastructure layer is not built for the inference pattern that test-time scaling produces.

  • High-throughput, low-latency test-time scaling. Repeated sampling, generation-to-generation updates, and tool calling differ sharply from mainstream single-turn chatbot traffic. This opens systems and inference-optimization work; the lab's efforts include Hydrogen and Tokamak, and they matter more as these methods go mainstream.
  • Hybrid serving engines. Route traffic smoothly between local and cloud models/accelerators depending on need and the complexity of the resources.
  • New architectures and kernels for energy-efficient inference, especially on local accelerators -- a much less studied area than cloud accelerators.
  • Energy as the primary resource. Metrics such as intelligence per watt, and better ways to measure and optimize watt and power usage, are expected to become mainstream target metrics.

Framing: the unleashed frontier sits at the intersection of fine-tuning, online learning, and test-time scaling, and it contains many unsolved challenges.

sections.title: Q&A: memory vs weights, infinite context, environments as proxies
sections.problem: If continual learning is the goal, should knowledge go into a long-term memory store or into the model weights? And do self-created environments actually proxy real-world tasks?
sections.why: An idealized infinite context that remembers and reasons over every experience does not exist -- reasoning over in-context data degrades within a few million tokens -- and a side memory store aids lookup but does not teach reasoning over new domains (a skill-transfer problem).
sections.how: Weights updates are needed for genuine skill transfer (e.g. cross-embodiment robot generalization), while memory-side approaches (databases, cartridge/KV-cache knowledge, massively longer context) avoid fine-tuning; environments matter only insofar as they proxy real-world feedback, which is easiest in finite spaces like games.
sections.detail:
Two audience questions clarify the continual-learning discussion.

Memory vs weights. An idealized infinite context that remembered every positive and negative experience and reasoned over all of it would be one answer -- but it does not exist, and reasoning over in-context (ICL) data diminishes within even a million or a few million tokens.

  • Alternatives without fine-tuning: update a memory store/database (the simplest naive version -- just update the DB), or use cartridge-style methods that bring knowledge into activations or KV caches and enable long-context ICL.
  • Trade-off: a side memory store is easier but does not teach reasoning over new domains; genuine skill transfer needs weight updates. Example: cross-embodiment robot generalization does not emerge from memory alone -- it is a skill-transfer problem.

Environments. For Absolute-Zero-style self-created environments, the point is not who authors them but whether they are reasonable proxies for real-world tasks. Easily simulated tasks are straightforward; finite spaces like games are easiest to represent in code and simulate.

sections.title: Closing remarks
sections.problem: The course ends and students must decide how to carry the material forward.
sections.why: The field moves fast enough that taught material becomes history within a year, but the underlying techniques compound because new work keeps building on them.
sections.how: Thank the class and point students toward their research projects, posters, and future work in self-improving agents.
sections.detail:
The instructors close the course with thanks.

  • The field is evolving so quickly that anything taught now starts becoming history by the next offering, but the basic techniques -- verifier-driven loops, RL and search, tool use, evaluation, and scaling -- remain valuable because new work still builds on them.
  • Students are pointed toward their research projects and posters as the place to push the open problems: reasoning diversity, robust and automated verification, data selection without a human bottleneck, synthetic-data flywheels, continual learning, and energy-efficient inference.
  • The second instructor notes the class was built while the instructors themselves were learning these fresh topics, and hopes it inspired new research directions.

End of the course.
